newsitem.title: USA: US lawmakers to urge mortgage insurance bill vote.
newsitem.headline: US lawmakers to urge mortgage insurance bill vote.

text.p: Democratic lawmakers backing a bill to curtail mortgage insurance plan to turn up the pressure on the Republican leadership to reschedule a vote on the measure.

The House of Representatives had scheduled a vote on the bill, H.R. 607 known as the Homeowners Insurance Protection Act, for April 8, but the vote was postponed and has not be rescheduled yet, congressional staffers said Thursday.
Passed by the House Banking Committee on a 36-to-one vote last month, the bill would allow homeowners to cancel mortgage insurance when they build up sufficient equity.

Currently, mortgage lenders require a borrower to obtain and pay for such insurance when the borrower is making a relatively small down payment, such as five percent of the purchase price of a home. Borrowers putting down 20 percent or more generally are not required to obtain insurance, which can cost $300 to $900 a year.

The bill would automatically cancel a mortgage insurance policy if the homewoner was current on mortgage payments and had built up 25 percent equity of the original value of the house. Homeowner's equity is the value of the home after subtracting the remaining amount of principal on the mortgage.
House Democrats said they planned to hold a press conference Thursday afternoon to call for a vote on the bill.

Both Democrats and Republicans voted for the measure in the House Banking Committee. Committee chairman Jim Leach of Iowa and Texas Rep. Henry Gonzalez, ranking Democrat on the panel, have both expressed support for the measure.

Consumer advocates also urged the House to schedule a vote. "It's really important that we not lose the momentum," Michelle Meier, counsel for government affairs at Consumers Union, said. "It would end an obviously unfair situation for homeowners."
Meier predicted the House would vote on the bill sometime next week. "I'm still optimistic that this is going to move forward," she said.
If the House passed the bill, focus would turn to the Senate where the Banking Committee has not yet voted on its version of the legislation.
Senate Banking Committee chairman Alfonse D'Amato, Republican of New York, has expressed strong support for the measure, but a committee session to amend and vote on a bill was postponed.
